cells.tense: The look arrives clean and you're standing where it lands — no hurry in it, no strain, the growing things in front of you met as they are.
cells.ask: Name one shape out loud this week to one person — a page, a pot, a mood — in a single sentence, and let it stand without asking anything back; that gives the shape a way to reach the person it belongs to.
cells.core:
You see the true shape of a thing before there are words for it. A mood crossing a face, a piece of work still deciding what it is — you notice it early and you work from there, which is why what you tend gets met at the stage it's actually in. That early arrival is the whole thing, and it's running clean right now.

Let it feed what's in front of you. Say one shape out loud this week — to a person, about a page, about a pot — and let the saying step past the last stage of deciding you meant to say it. What this opens isn't more insight than you have; it's the shape reaching the person it belongs to.

cells.tense: You're already at next season — reading the version of this that hasn't grown yet and meeting that instead of what's on the bench in front of you.
cells.ask: Pick one thing this week and look at it before you fix it — no next step, no plan, no correcting — for a full slow minute; that gives a version that gets to be exactly the size it is.
cells.core:
Attentive, this is a plain and generous way to be: a person, a page, a pot, met at the stage they're actually in, no finishing moved back onto them before they're ready. That's the rest inside caring for what's growing. When it runs hot, the look races ahead — a decision someone hasn't made gets read as made, a piece still forming gets corrected as if it already came out — and the care gets spent on a story no one told yet.

Look at one current thing long enough to see it as it stands. The draft as it is. The person as they are today. The pot with the yellow leaf. Leave the future where it belongs and let this be enough for one sitting. What this opens is a look with nothing bracing in it, and a thing that got to be its current size.

cells.tense: The look has gone quiet and the bench is running on an old print — the shape a thing had last time, still being tended as if it were the one here now.
cells.ask: Watch one person for one full minute this week without doing anything for them — no fix, no next step — and let what you actually see in that minute decide the next move; that gives contact with the live version, on ground you can stand on.
cells.core:
This is generous attention at its plainest: what's in front of you, whatever stage it's in, worked from what's actually there — a mood before it swells, a version still forming, a person met where they are. When nothing new is arriving, that same line keeps running on an old read — the person as they were, the task as it stood — and the care gets spent on a shape nobody can reach anymore.

The fix is small and concrete. One person, one full minute, no fixing while you watch. What this opens is a look with live ground under it — not a grade on the care, just the next true thing in front of you.

cells.tense: The look runs unnamed — catching the shape of a room, a person, a piece of work before anyone asks — and it gets handed back as simply how things are.
cells.ask: Say one read out loud this week: what you noticed, and that it was you who noticed it — one sentence, about one thing on the bench; that gives a clean look with a name on it instead of an anonymous fact.
cells.core:
When this works, catching shape early is what lets you move through a room without anyone having to explain it — you spot the fight before it cracks open, the version of the work still deciding, the mood that hasn't been spoken. That quiet service is real and it lands, and nothing about it needs proving.

The piece that's missing is whose read it is. This week, catch one of those shapes while it's still small — a mood, a version, a person's real state — and say to yourself what you see and that it's what you see. Then look at the same thing again. The room doesn't change. The ownership does.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim in my draft risked saying the person keeps things small or hides what they see, which the record does not establish; the reader may reasonably say this isn't about hiding or holding back at all. So the cells locate the condition in what the person's seeing is doing right now — meeting a thing already finished, treating a nameable scene as still forming, switching off a registered sight — without any story of why or how long. The asks are ordinary visible acts (say where someone is, cross a nail polish off, walk the route and name the first thing) and they stay useful even if the reading is wrong about which capacity is starved. The sentence that served the writer rather than the reader was any line implying the person was letting a seedling die; I cut it — the cells keep the sleeping seed as a possibility, never a verdict on their care.
